text: Cassini did this for planetary protection, not because Saturn itself is a life target. The worry was that after the orbiters and probes had done their work, a dead spacecraft could slowly wander and hit a moon. Enceladus and Titan were the big concerns, since both might have conditions where microbes could survive. A controlled plunge into Saturn gets destroyed in the upper atmosphere, which takes the hardware out of the system. It is a bit awkward to send a working probe straight into a gas giant, but the alternative, letting it drift, is messier, so they chose the crash.

Your stationary leg is doing more than just standing. It has to take the board's weight, correct balance, and absorb every bump and pop from the street. If you're always using the same stance, that leg is the one doing the quiet work of stabilizing while the other leg pumps. Over time the muscles around the knee and ankle get tired and tight, and you feel it as a dull ache. That is a bit silly, but it is also common.

I would look at how you set your feet before anything else. A stance that is too narrow puts the stationary leg into a slightly unstable position, so the small muscles in your shin and calf have to fight harder to keep you upright. If the board is too long or the wheels too hard, every little crack in the pavement goes straight up into that leg. Sometimes the pain means you are leaning too far toward it or letting it absorb shocks the board should absorb.

One thing to check is whether the hurt is in the ankle, knee, or calf. If it is right over the knee cap, you may be locking that leg instead of keeping it slightly bent. A little bend keeps the joint from taking the full jolt. If it is deeper, in the ankle, it is likely from the repeated twisting or landing pressure on a single side.

I wouldn't bother changing your board or shoes until you have looked at your feet first. Most of the time, the fix is simpler than new gear. Try standing with your stationary knee loose and your weight centered, then skate briefly and see if the ache changes. If it gets worse when you land or push off, the problem is the shock your leg is forced to take, not an injury.

The label is more about shared history than about where a person was born. Most Black Americans descend from people brought from Africa, whether from West Africa, Central Africa, or elsewhere, and that connection is what the name points to. It doesn't mean every single person was born on the African continent or can name a specific village. The term African American, or the older Afro-American, groups people around the experience of being Black in America, the slave trade, segregation, and the communities that grew up around it. You'll see it on passports, surveys, and community organizations, and people often use it as shorthand for the Black American experience rather than as an origin certificate. Some people do trace direct family roots to Africa, but many more are simply part of the broader Black American population. It's not a genealogical proof. A person can identify as African American without ever having lived in Africa, and that's a big part of why the label feels odd to outsiders. The word is a cultural and historical identifier, not a claim about current residence. I'd say it's meant to signal shared heritage, not to assert that most of them are actually from Africa today.

Mostly local black markets and smuggled stock. People buy from dealers in the bazaars, from captured weapons from fallen fighters, and from regional flows that move through border gaps. A few rifles also come from old state stores that got looted when units broke up. You get them because someone across the line has a gun, and if you can make money by selling or leasing a weapon, you keep doing it. Factions also want a fighting force, not just a sidearm. They still arm because no one trusts anyone.

I wouldn't put it as all drugs are bad. It's the strong part that drags the bad parts along. A medicine that barely touches you is nearly safe, and a drug that makes you feel very good is working hard on the same circuits that also do sleep, hunger, heartbeat and breathing. That's the part people miss. If it gives you intense euphoria, it has changed something in your brain, and your body will push back. You get less of the high the more often you take it, and you need more to get the same feeling. That's just how these systems behave.

The word you're circling is pleasure, but the effect is never just pleasure. Opioids slow breathing and dry the mouth, coke raises the heart rate and wrecks sleep. Even a mild one can have a cost if used often. What makes a drug useful is the same change that makes it risky. The brain keeps adjusting itself, so the high fades faster each time. You don't have to be a heavy user to feel it, and you don't have to be one to feel the downsides.

A drug that gives intense pleasure is not a switch you turn on and off cleanly. It nudges the nervous system, and the nervous system fights the nudge. That nudge can also disturb sleep, appetite, hormones, and the way you think. None of that is the point of taking the drug, but it's what you actually get. If the high is intense, the side effects are unlikely to be zero, because intensity needs a real change in the brain's reward chemistry, and the body responds by trying to restore balance. The brain does have one technical mechanism here, called dopamine signaling, and it is tied to the same reward, learning and motivation systems that keep you alive. You don't need to understand the science fully, just know that the systems are not separated by a clean wall.

A drug strong enough to produce intense pleasure also has to be strong enough to disturb the systems that keep the body steady. Zero adverse effects would mean it barely did anything, or that the costs only showed up later, and those are not the same thing. The more dramatic the high, the harder the body pushes back. (Which is a bit silly if you want a perfect pleasure pill.)

Hi,

The physical pain is probably in your feet, legs, and lower back, not your head. Shopping with your wife means walking for hours, carrying bags, and waiting. That strain shows up as soreness, not a normal headache. You are not imagining it. Your legs do most of the work. It is a real physical toll, and the aching makes sense. I would check your shoes first. Bad or tight shoes can make it worse. If the pain gets sharp or keeps you from walking, see someone. Sit whenever you can and keep the day shorter next time.

Thanks

Hi,
Your mind probably jumped to milk because cows and milk are the pair most people connect. The silk repeating and spelling put you into a word game, so when your brother asked what cows drink, the easy answer came out before you could catch it. That is a normal automatic response. The question is a gotcha, because it asks about drinking, but milk is what cows are famous for. You were not confused about water. The milk answer got there first. I would not read too much into a slip. If it happened during a cognitive test, it may be a priming effect. If he was being playful, it was a trick question. Either way, your brain took the shortcut, and you noticed the mismatch with water. It is more about attention sticking to the word task. Do not treat this as a sign of anything at all.
Thanks

Hi,

You haven't given me much to go on with just a subject line, so I'm guessing what you're stuck on. Two big ones: don't skip the survey and don't get too greedy with your budget. Get an independent surveyor to look at the house before you complete; you'll avoid nasty surprises with damp or structural issues. And don't stretch yourself too thin on the mortgage. You want a little breathing room in case interest rates move or you have a bad month. If it's a 3-in-1 suite or something similar, check the service charges carefully. I wouldn't bother worrying about the exact paint colour or the garden right now. Let me know what specific questions you have.

Thanks

Hi,

For hair, a 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner is not a mix of the three products, it is one formula made to do all three jobs. The washing part cleans your skin and hair, while the extra ingredients keep your hair from feeling stripped. A regular shampoo is a cleaning product, and the 3-in-1 also softens hair. Compared with a 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner, the 3-in-1 is also meant for the whole body, so it is milder for skin and less aggressively foaming.

The catch is that you are getting a compromise. It will clean your hair and give it a bit of slip, but it will not condition as well as a dedicated conditioner. If your main concern is hair, a separate shampoo and conditioner will usually do a better job. For the body, the 3-in-1 is fine if you want one bottle for washing everything, and I would not expect it to replace your favorite body wash for dry patches. Do not overuse it on hair if your scalp is sensitive, and do not expect the body side to be as hydrating as a lotion. For dry or damaged hair, use a separate conditioner afterwards. It is a convenience product, not a full replacement.

Thanks

You can pin down a continent's speed by putting GPS receivers on solid ground and comparing their positions over months or years. The receiver gives a latitude, longitude, and height, and by looking at how far and in what direction that spot has shifted, you get a rate in centimetres per year. That is the direct measurement.

The numbers are smaller than you might think. Continents usually crawl a few centimetres each year, which is why the measurements have to run long enough to separate real movement from the normal drift in one receiver. The positions are also corrected for the ground under your feet moving with the ice sheet or the local earth deformation, because those can look like continent motion when they are not.

For the longer picture, they also look at the sea floor. New rock forms at the ridge, and as it moves away from the ridge you can measure its distance from the ridge and use the rock's age to infer the spreading rate. That gives the same kind of number, but over millions of years rather than months.

The GPS result is the one I would trust for current speed. The geological record checks it over a much longer span.

Thanks

Inbreeding does not mean relatives deliberately pass bad genes to each other. It means shared ancestors make it more likely that two copies of the same harmful gene meet in a child.

Many genes have small effects on intelligence. Some rare recessive mutations hurt brain development or cause illness. A child can inherit the same harmful copy from both parents, and that is where the damage shows up. Closely related parents raise the chance of recessive problems, including some that lower cognitive ability. It is the same logic as a hidden family health problem surfacing when two carriers meet.

The lower IQ is not one switch. It is the accumulated result of more harmful copies appearing. The child's brain may develop normally in many ways, but certain functions end up weaker than average. The effect is probabilistic, not guaranteed for every child. That is the basic science.

If you get hit, shot, or stabbed in the arm, it often hurts less than the same injury to the stomach or chest. The arm has a good layer of muscle and fat, and fewer vital structures packed into the space. A bullet or blade tends to meet soft tissue first, and the arm's nerves are spread out over a wider area than, say, the back of the neck. That makes the first shock feel smaller, and it gives you more room before anything critical is reached.

You may also notice that it does not seem to hurt as much as you expect. People often underestimate an arm wound until it bleeds, swells, or the arm goes numb or weak. If the pain is sharp, throbbing, or getting worse, treat it as real, even if you feel fine at first. If the arm is cold or the pulse feels weak, get checked.

Carbon monoxide steals the oxygen your blood is supposed to carry to your brain. It binds to the hemoglobin in your red blood cells, which is the protein that transports oxygen. The catch is that carbon monoxide grabs that protein about 200 times tighter than oxygen does. Once it locks on, your body can't easily get it off. That leaves you short of oxygen while you are still breathing perfectly fine air. You can be standing in a room that smells completely normal, but your blood is already carrying the gas to your organs.

Carbon dioxide does not do this. It is the waste gas your cells produce, and your lungs clear it out with every breath you take. You do not need a mask for normal air with a little carbon dioxide in it. Carbon monoxide is a different problem. It is colorless and odorless, which is a bit of a trap (I would not want to rely on your nose to warn you). A small concentration is enough to make you dizzy or nauseous, and higher levels can knock you out before you can leave the room.

The real danger is how quietly it happens. You might be sitting at your desk or working near the boiler room. You feel fine at first. Then your vision blurs and your head starts to ache. By the time you realize something is wrong, your blood is saturated with the gas. It is not a fast killer like a fire, but it quietly starves your brain of the oxygen it needs. That is the core difference between the two gases. If you are ever in the mechanical wing, you should know that the red alarm means the detectors found the gas. Get to fresh air immediately. Do not use your phone or strike a match near the boiler until maintenance checks the system. Keep your distance from the source until they clear the room.

When an aircraft must brace for impact, the crew asks you to lower your head, press it against the seat back, bend your knees, and keep your feet flat on the floor if you can. The position is not comfortable, but it is the position that reduces injury. In a sudden stop, your body would otherwise keep moving. The compact position limits how far your head, chest, and legs can go.

This matters most for the neck and chest. The neck is protected because the head is braced against the seat, not swinging forward. The chest and spine are protected because the legs are bent and the hands are held on the shins or on your knees. In a crash or very rough turbulence, those soft points are kept away from hard surfaces as much as possible. The bent knees also help keep the pelvis and shins from striking the seat frame.

You do not need to be strong to do this correctly. You need to follow the crew instructions and hold the position until they say it is safe. That simple, repeated action is what makes the difference. Cabin crew demonstrate this in safety videos.

You'll find old trading houses and family workshops, not the big names you see today. Most were small and local, and they rarely kept the same name, owner, or product line long enough to become famous. The industrial era changed that. Mass production, standardized packaging, and wider distribution let a company reach far more customers, and those conditions produced the names you know now. A handful of older firms may have earlier roots, but their fame usually comes from what they did after the change. (It is a bit silly to expect every old shop to become a global brand.)

I keep running into the same confusion about how a bank can be cheaper when the dealership quotes a lower interest rate. For me, the answer is that the rate is not the price. The dealer's headline rate is a sales number. What I pay is the whole package. Dealerships use a low rate to pull you in, then build cost into fees and add-ons. You can end up paying for dealer prep, documentation, and an optional package you never asked for, all while the loan looks better than the bank's rate. That gap is where the dealer makes it back.

A bank, by contrast, usually gives you a rate and a fee, and then leaves you alone. I do not mean every dealer is sneaky. I mean the structure invites comparison to be unfair. If the dealer is offering a subsidized rate, that subsidy usually comes with conditions. It may be limited to a short term, a particular model, or a specific loan amount. When those conditions do not fit your purchase, the dealer often has to add charges to keep the deal balanced. The bank does not need to recover a rate subsidy the same way.

There is also the payoff problem. I have seen dealers handle early payoff inconsistently, and that inconsistency can cost you. A bank usually states the payoff amount plainly. If you plan to pay off early, ask both for the exact payoff at month six or month twelve. That number matters more than the advertised rate.

My position is that the lower rate is real but narrow. The dealer wins on the paper, not on the total. I would rather accept a slightly higher bank rate and know the final amount owed. The bank may quote a number you can check against your own budget, without a stack of optional charges attached. That transparency is worth something. I have learned to read the fine print, and to compare apples to apples. A low rate can still hide extra charges.

So when someone tells me the dealer rate is lower, I ask about the total. I look at the monthly payment, the fees, the term, and any add-ons. I keep the same loan terms for both quotes. I would not assume a low rate means a cheap loan. It usually means the dealer is using the rate as a hook, and the real cost is buried in the details.

Here's the thing I keep running into: being legal in your state doesn't mean you're legal to the feds. I live in a state where the pot is openly sold, and I've been smoking for years, and I can tell you the DEA still treats it like it's heroin-class. That federal Schedule I label is the whole problem, and nobody really talks about it (which is a bit silly). So you can buy a gram in the state, but then file federal taxes where it counts as a business expense, and now you've got to think about the 280A carve-out. I think the states are right to move fast. The federal government is stuck in its own bureaucratic inertia, which is why I'd bet on the states to keep winning, even if Congress is still arguing. That gap is where most of the confusion lives. I keep seeing the gap grow, not shrink.

I find it hard to take the question of bodily electricity as exotic. The practical point is that our cells run on charged salts moving through membranes, not some hidden generator. A nerve signal happens when sodium rushes in and potassium leaves, and that little voltage change is what you feel as a twitch or a thought. I won't explain every pump or channel here. The part I care about is that ordinary ions moving is the actual electricity, and your heart and muscles are doing it at scale. Less like lightning, more like a million tiny circuits staying balanced.

I think sampling is less about stealing and more about putting old music into a new context. The practical part is the same for most people who do it. You find a record, tape, or digital file with a phrase you want to use. In my case, I keep a pile of vinyl and old CDs and I listen with the goal of finding a drum break, a bass line, or a vocal hook that feels alive in a way my own playing does not. That first listen is often the hardest part, because you are not just looking for a melody, you are listening for texture, a syncopated rhythm, a specific timbre, or a moment that makes the track suddenly interesting.

Once you have the snippet, you get the audio into software or hardware. You might rip a CD, digitize a tape, or cut the phrase straight off the record. From there, the sample is chopped into small pieces, then rearranged. A short drum break can be looped, a bass line can be pitched down or sped up, and a vocal phrase can be stretched, reversed, or drenched in delay. I often use a sampler or a DAW, set the loop points carefully, and then push the tempo until the old recording fits the new arrangement. The detail matters here. If the loop does not line up with the beat, the whole track sounds off. So I listen to each transition and nudge the trim points.

The second half is not just sound, it is permissions. Using an older song does not mean you automatically own the result. In practice, people contact the rights holders, negotiate a license, or settle for a cleared sample with restrictions. If you are making something for a club night, a live set, or just practice, you may not worry about paperwork. If you plan to release commercially, the legal side becomes the part everyone forgets. I would rather find a track that is clearly owned by one label than argue over a split between a composer, a performer, and a record company later.

What I enjoy most is the transformation. An old soul record can become a modern beat without pretending the original was not there. The sample carries a little of the past into the present, but the new music still needs to work on its own terms. That is the point.

Most people think a headache is the brain hurting, but the brain itself doesn't feel pain. I take the position that the pain comes from the things wrapped around it, the skull lining, scalp, and blood vessels near the head. When I get one, I stop and note the tightness or throbbing. That usually means a blood vessel is under stress or a nerve is being pulled, not that my thoughts are literally aching.

The concrete bit matters. If the pain sits high behind the eyes, I tend to suspect the eye strain or the sinuses. If it throbs along the temple, it feels more like vessel-related stress. I don't need a dramatic answer. A headache is the body's alarm system, and the alarm is wired into the outer parts of the head, not the inner thought factory. I treat that as a practical clue, not a medical diagnosis, usually.

I can’t even tell you if the food is good, because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, choosing this place specifically because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and figured it’d be easy. We put our names on their completely pointless digital waitlist. They told us to come back to pay at 8:23. We did, but then just stood around until 8:40 before staff casually said we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15. It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past payment, tell people up front so our night isn’t completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. For two people it came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned it actually cost somewhat more than I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that no steak was offered. At that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices were lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station was not especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any.

I’d call the whole thing acceptable but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably think twice.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of my thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it still stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version of it, so I’ve sat through lots of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally saw, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe a little worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re looking down into it, so from nearly any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too: the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. A lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not a rip-off exactly, just that if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never told me what it was trying to say. Also, too much was happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. It felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal: $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. A few friends actually liked it, though. If you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The shirts never arrived because the sales rep recorded the delivery address wrong, and her handwritten “7” was read as a “1.” It was meant to go to 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people living there took it to the local UPS store for return. The package disappeared and we never heard anything more. It was several weeks before we found out. While that was being disputed, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount would not refund the original two. The owner handled it at that point. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly to blame because we had not been friendly enough to the people at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually got a credit.
